sources.title: The New Cambridge History of India
An Atlas of the Mughal Empire
sources.author: Irfan Habib

claims.note: The Mamluk sultans held the Doab and the Punjab. Expansion south comes later.
Khalji and early Tughlaq maximum. Gujarat taken 1299. Southern conquests were raids and short-lived tributary arrangements rather than settled territory, so they are not drawn as held.
Contraction under the later Tughlaqs. Bengal gone 1352, the Deccan gone 1347, Gujarat and Malwa going.

Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 and the sultanate did not recover under the Sayyids. Contemporaries joked that their writ ran from Delhi to Palam. Drawn as the capital and the upper doab; the Punjab governors, Jaunpur, Malwa and Gujarat were gone.
Bahlul Lodi rebuilt the sultanate from Sirhind, took Jaunpur in 1479, and Sikandar Lodi pushed into Bihar. The Lodis held the Punjab and the plain again until Panipat.
Babur and Humayun held the Doab and the Punjab, and Humayun lost even that to Sher Shah between 1540 and 1555.
Akbar's empire: Gujarat 1573, Bengal 1576, the whole northern plain.
Jahangir and Shah Jahan held the northern plain. The Deccan war ran for decades without the sultanates falling, so their ground is not drawn as Mughal here.

replaces.name: Bengal
replaces.reason: Akbar annexed Bengal in 1576 and it was a Mughal suba throughout this period. The boundary source goes on drawing it as an independent state.

replaces.name: Orissa
replaces.reason: Annexed by Akbar in 1592 and governed from Bengal. The source still draws it separately.

claims.note: Bijapur fell in 1686 and Golconda in 1687, bringing the Deccan plateau under Aurangzeb. The far south below the Krishna was never held.

replaces.name: Bidar
replaces.reason: Taken by Bijapur in 1619 and Mughal with it in 1686.

claims.note: The peninsula south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra. The doab between the two rivers was contested with the Bahmanis throughout and is not separately drawn.

replaces.name: Chola Empire
replaces.reason: The Chola line ended in 1279, when the Pandyas took Gangaikonda Cholapuram. The boundary source carries the label into the fifteenth century; this ground was Vijayanagara's from the 1340s.

replaces.name: Pandya state
replaces.reason: The Pandya kingdom broke apart after the Madurai sultanate seized its capital in 1335, and Vijayanagara took Madurai in 1378. The source still draws a Pandya state in 1400.

claims.note: After Talikota the empire survived at Penukonda and Chandragiri with its nayakas increasingly independent. Drawn as the same ground because the successor nayaka states are not yet modelled separately.
Broke from Delhi in 1347 and held the Deccan between the Krishna and the Tapti until the five successor sultanates divided it.
Independent of Delhi from Ilyas Shah's unification until the Mughal conquest.
Zafar Khan governed Gujarat from 1391; Muzaffar Shah I declared independence from the Tughlaqs in 1394 and the line took the sultan's title in 1407. The claim starts at the declaration.
Independent of Delhi from 1392 until Akbar annexed it.
The Sharqi sultanate held Awadh and the eastern plain from Delhi's collapse until the Lodis took it back.
The Eastern Gangas held the same coast before the Gajapatis, and were never under Delhi.
The Gajapatis held the Kalinga coast from the Mahanadi toward the Godavari.

The Sisodia state in the southern Aravallis — Chittor until 1568, then Udaipur. Marwar, Amber, Bikaner and Jaisalmer were separate Rajput states and are left to the boundary source rather than folded into this one.
The Sammas ruled the lower Indus from Thatta, independent of Delhi.

Scindia held Delhi from 1788 with the Mughal emperor as a pensioner, until the Second Anglo-Maratha War of 1803-05 brought the country around Delhi into direct Company rule. The source separates the Marathas into two features at 1783 -- Mahratta states in the north around Delhi and Gwalior, and the Maratha Confederacy in the Deccan -- and at 1800 only the Deccan one survives. This borrows the northern one.

The Deccan and central-India half of the same claim. It exists because a claim supersedes the source's feature of that polity's name: without restating this, repairing Delhi would have deleted Pune, Nagpur and Cuttack. Borrowed from 1783 rather than 1800 because the 1783 feature also covers Allahabad, Rewa and Baghelkhand, which the Marathas still held in 1800 and lost to the Company in 1803 -- the 1800 feature has already shed them to the mislabelled blob.

The nawabs held Awadh from 1722 to 1856 and the source draws Oudh at both 1783 and 1815 -- only the 1800 snapshot loses it. Extent borrowed from 1783, before the 1801 treaty took half the territory, which is the right side of that change for 1800.

The company governed Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from the diwani of 1765. The source draws Bengal at 1783 and the British East India Company at 1815; at 1800 it draws neither. Extent borrowed from 1783 rather than 1815, because the 1815 shape already includes Delhi and the ceded provinces, which the company did not hold in 1800.

Ajit Singh recovered Jodhpur after Aurangzeb's death and Marwar was not administered from Delhi again. The boundary source draws Mughal Empire over Jodhpur at 1715, 1783, 1800 and 1815; it was a Rathore state throughout, and a Maratha tributary rather than a Mughal province for much of the later stretch. Extent is the districts the Marwar article names, with Mewar cut out. Bikaner and Jaisalmer are not claimed.

The Namgyal dynasty article has the kingdom lasting 1460 to 1842 with conflicts against the NEIGHBOURING Mughal Empire -- neighbouring, so Leh was never inside it. The source draws Mughal Empire over Leh at 1715, Lahore at 1783, Afghanistan at 1800 and the Maratha Confederacy at 1815. None of those held Ladakh. It fell to the Dogras in 1842.

The Ahom kingdom article calls it a kingdom of the Brahmaputra Valley, 1228 to 1826. The source draws Shan states over Garhgaon from 1530 to 1715 and Burma at 1783 and 1800, which puts Assam in the wrong country -- the dynasty was of Tai origin but the kingdom was not a Shan state, and Assam was not Burmese until the invasions after 1817. It stops at 1806 because the source names Assam itself at 1815. The claim starts at 1671, after Saraighat settled the Mughal question; the earlier centuries are left alone because the western frontier with the Koch and the Mughals moved and this file cannot yet say where.

Chhatrasal was Maharaja of Bundelkhand from 1675 to 1731 and the article is explicit that he led its independence from the Mughals. The source draws Mughal Empire over Orchha at 1715. Extent is the country between the Yamuna and the Vindhyas.

The Wodeyars declared independence from a collapsing Vijayanagara in the sixteenth century and Srirangapatna was the seat from 1610. The source draws Vijayanagara over Mysore at 1650, sixty years after the Wodeyars broke with it and four after Vijayanagara itself ended, and Hindu kingdoms at 1700 and 1715. It stops at 1760 because from 1783 the source names Mysore itself, and draws it larger than this box -- Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan took Malabar and the south, and where the source is right the claim layer has no business overwriting it with something smaller.

The Seuna article gives the realm at its peak as stretching from the Narmada in the north to the Tungabhadra in the south, in the western Deccan, from Devagiri. The boundary source names no Yadava state in any year and draws minor Hindu kingdoms and Rajput kingdoms over Devagiri instead -- the second of which is not even the right part of India.

The Kakatiya article gives the reach as most of the eastern Deccan, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh with parts of eastern Karnataka, northern Tamil Nadu and southern Odisha, from Orugallu, now Warangal. The source draws minor Hindu kingdoms and Rajput kingdoms there. The box stops at 77.4E where the Seuna claim begins, so the two Deccan powers do not overlap.

The Satavahana article names Pratishthana, which is Paithan, and Amaravati as capitals at different times; the claim holds both. The source draws the Saka kingdom over Paithan in three of these four snapshots and the Mauryan empire in the fourth, eighty-five years after the Mauryas ended.

note: Claims are ordered broad to specific. A later claim cuts every earlier one it overlaps, so the file order states which power holds contested ground.

scope.note: The ground and period this file speaks for. It is a statement of scope, not a licence: where no claim here covers the ground, the boundary source stands. An earlier version treated it as authority and erased everything the source drew inside it, which removed Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, the Gond kingdoms, the Rajput states and the Sinhalese kingdoms from 1492. Extended past 1707 because stopping at Aurangzeb's death left the eighteenth century to the source alone, and the source draws five names over the whole subcontinent in 1715: Mughal Empire, Maratha, Hindu kingdoms, Shan states and Tibet. Marwar, Ladakh and Bundelkhand fell inside the Mughal blob and Assam inside the Shan one.
